subtitle.en: Bantu Grammar, Endangered Manuscripts and the Swahili Classroom

meta.en: Role: Teaching Associate Professor and Language Coordinator, Department of African, African American, and Diaspora Studies, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Region: Chapel Hill, USA; trained in Kenya (Egerton University) and the United States
Field: Swahili corpus linguistics and pragmatics, African language pedagogy, African literatures, manuscript preservation
Education: PhD in Linguistics (University of Texas at Arlington, 2014); MA in Languages and Linguistics and Bachelor of Education (Egerton University, Kenya)

blocks.en: In a department at one of America's leading public universities, a Kenyan-trained linguist teaches students to speak Swahili. He also studies the grammar of Bantu languages using large digital collections of real text, and he has helped digitise thousands of pages of endangered African manuscripts. Mohamed Mwamzandi's career follows a path less visible than political leadership but important for the future of languages like Chidigo: scholarship applied to documenting, teaching and preserving African languages.

*A note on background:* the Chidigo project has not been able to confirm from public sources whether Dr Mwamzandi is Digo or where on the Kenya coast, if anywhere, he calls home. This article does not make that claim. The project would welcome his own account.
From Egerton to Chapel Hill

Mwamzandi earned his Bachelor of Education and his Master of Arts in Languages and Linguistics at **Egerton University** in Kenya. He then completed a Certificate in African Language Pedagogy at the National African Language Resource Center at **Indiana University Bloomington** [1]. In 2014 he received his PhD in Linguistics from the **University of Texas at Arlington**. His dissertation, *Swahili Word Order Choices: Insights from Information Structure*, was supervised by a committee of Laurel Smith Stvan, Joseph Sabbagh, Jeffrey Witzel and Jason Kandybowicz [2].

He joined the faculty at **UNC Chapel Hill** and was listed as Teaching Assistant Professor by 2018 [3]. He is now Teaching Associate Professor and Language Coordinator in the Department of African, African American, and Diaspora Studies. He teaches elementary and intermediate Kiswahili, Introduction to the Languages of Africa, and Introduction to African Literature [1].

His teaching philosophy treats Swahili as a gateway. His departmental profile has described Swahili as a lingua franca spoken across Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi, Burundi, Rwanda, Congo, Mozambique and Somalia. It also stated that "studying Swahili is a gateway to learning the over 400 Bantu languages spoken in Africa because of the close genetic relationship between these languages" [3]. On this view Swahili is an entry point rather than a destination, which implicitly supports the study and preservation of related Bantu languages such as Chidigo.
Research: Grammar from Real Language

**Corpus linguistics and pragmatics.** Mwamzandi's linguistic research asks why Swahili speakers choose one grammatical form over an apparently equivalent one. To answer it, he works with the **Helsinki Corpus of Swahili**, a large electronic collection of naturally occurring text, and analyses thousands of real examples statistically [2][3]. His dissertation showed two things. When a demonstrative follows the noun (*mtu huyu*), it usually refers to something already active in the conversation. When it comes first (*huyu mtu*), it brings back a topic that had faded. In reciprocal constructions, "givenness, rather than verb category, is the main predictor" of word order [2]. He later applied the same method to Swahili conditionals and to the choice between *amba-* relative clauses and tensed relative clauses [4][6].

This is technical Bantu linguistics. It also shows the kind of annotated, corpus-based description that dictionaries, grammars, teaching materials and language technologies all need. Chidigo is a close relative of Swahili and still has little of that infrastructure. His departmental profile has listed computational linguistics among his research areas [3]. His published work so far is corpus-based grammatical analysis rather than software or language models.

**Endangered manuscripts.** Mwamzandi has also worked directly on preserving African written heritage. With his UNC colleague Samba Camara and the West African Research Center, he led a project funded by the **British Library's Endangered Archives Programme** (US$45,000). In 2018–19 the team digitised Pulaar *Ajami* (Arabic-script) Islamic manuscripts by Haalpulaar scholars of the Tijaniyya tradition in Senegal and Mali, about 6,000 pages in all. Many of the manuscripts were written in a locally made ink called *daha*, and they were vulnerable to water, fire, termites and mould [1][7][8]. The project is a working model of what rescuing a language's written record involves. That lesson applies directly to the scattered Digo-language texts, recordings and manuscripts of Kwale and Tanga.

**Language, religion and security.** His profile has described work on "counter violent extremism efforts in Africa and how the use of local languages and involvement of the target communities may help in the war against terror." He presented a paper on "The role of Swahili language in the Kenya government counter terrorism efforts" at the Southeast African Languages and Literatures Forum [3]. His current research agenda covers religious extremism, ideology and human rights in Kenya. With Raphael Birya, he has studied how Kenyan churches and mosques used social media during the COVID-19 pandemic [1][9].
Key Publications

***Swahili Word Order Choices: Insights from Information Structure*** (PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington, 2014) — corpus and questionnaire study of demonstratives and reciprocals [2].

**"A corpus study of Swahili conditionals"** (*Studies in African Linguistics* 46(1), 2017) — finds that the conditional markers *-ki-* and *ikiwa* carry no fixed pragmatic implicature, although *-ki-* is more frequent in content and speech-act conditionals and *ikiwa* in epistemic ones [4][10].
**"A corpus study of the Swahili demonstrative position"** (in *African Linguistics on the Prairie*, Language Science Press, 2018; open access) [5].

**"The pragmatics of Swahili relative clauses"** (in *Descriptive and Theoretical Approaches to African Linguistics*, Contemporary African Linguistics series, 2022) — uses 440 relative clauses from the Helsinki Corpus [1][6].

**"Arabic and Pulaar Manuscripts in Senegal and Mali"** (with Samba Camara, in *Manuscripts and Arabic-script Writing in Africa*, The Islamic Manuscript Association and Bibliotheca Alexandrina, 2023) [1].

Co-editor, with Samba Camara, of ***African Languages, Literatures, and Postcolonial Modernity*** (Cambridge Scholars Publishing, 2024). The book looks at how African languages and literatures, in novels, film, poetry and music, have carried and mediated modernity. His chapter in it is "Language Instruction, Intercultural Competence and STEM Research in Africa" [1][11].
**"Religious Institutions' Use of Social Media Platforms During COVID-19 in Kenya"** (with Raphael Birya, *Social Media + Society* 11(3), 2025) [1][9].

Co-editor, with Raphael Birya, of ***The Dynamics of Mobility in African Languages and Literatures: Opportunities and Challenges*** (Bloomsbury, 2026). Its twelve chapters cover Afro-diasporic literature, postcolonial resistance, and the resilience of African languages [1][12].
Cross-Cultural Language Education

At UNC, Mwamzandi leads teaching and research collaborations with **Pwani University** in Kilifi, on the Kenya coast, through **Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL)**. These collaborations link students across the two institutions for shared learning. He has received a UNC Global Affairs Global Partnership Expansion Grant for this work [1]. Classroom partnerships of this kind, using technology to bring learners and speakers together across continents, are a model that could one day connect Chidigo learners in the diaspora with speakers in Kwale and Tanga.
Legacy

Mohamed Mwamzandi does not, in his published work, focus on the Digo language. His relevance to the Digo linguistic future lies in what his work builds and models. His corpus studies show how a Bantu language's grammar can be described from real usage. His manuscript project shows how endangered written heritage can be rescued and made public. His classroom partnership with a coastal Kenyan university is one more instance of East African linguistics at a major research university. Every corpus-based grammar study, every digitised manuscript and every student who learns that Africa's 400-plus Bantu languages deserve serious study helps a language like Chidigo find its way into the digital world rather than being left behind.

A Digo proverb runs *"Mvula igodzwa na utseru"*: the rain is waited for with a cleared plot. Mwamzandi's work is a kind of plot-clearing. It builds methods, trains people and lays the intellectual groundwork that will be needed when the time comes to carry Chidigo fully into the 21st century.
